_Why can lifetime inference cost dwarf training cost?_

Training is paid for each model version; serving continues throughout that version's operational lifetime. A model trained for millions of dollars may serve billions of requests, each consuming compute, memory, network, and energy. At high traffic, recurring inference expense can exceed the original training cost by orders of magnitude. Milliseconds of latency and small differences in accelerator utilization then compound across the service's lifetime. A fast prediction measured on an otherwise idle machine does not reveal how the same model behaves when requests arrive together, vary in length, and compete for memory. Work can spend longer waiting than executing, while an apparently busy fleet produces responses that arrive too late to be useful. Keeping extra machines ready protects response time but incurs cost during quiet periods; admitting more work improves utilization only while the service can still meet its promises. Failures sharpen this tension because displaced requests consume the spare capacity intended to absorb demand changes. Continuing to accept work during overload can worsen the shortage when delayed requests trigger retries that compete for capacity. The engineering decision is therefore how much useful work the fleet can sustain at an acceptable cost while preserving response quality and timeliness. The answer depends on the request mix and service requirements, so a gain for one workload may become a loss for another. In C³ terms, compute reuse must pay for communication and coordination without exhausting the user's latency budget.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Estimate lifetime serving cost from traffic volume, deployment duration, and measured cost per SLO-compliant request
- Select batching, scheduling, and per-request compute-budget policies for vision, LLM, recommender, and streaming workloads
- Analyze attention-cache capacity, fragmentation, and prefill-decode interference under workload-dependent serving constraints
- Compare sharding, disaggregation, and quantized serving designs using communication, memory, and quality constraints
- Evaluate routing, overload-control, and isolation policies against tail latency, retry amplification, and noisy-neighbor risks
- Design autoscaling and multi-region routing policies that balance cold starts, cost, and SLO compliance
- Synthesize serving architectures that manage C³ trade-offs across request, replica, service, and platform layers

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: inference-setup
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INFERENCE CHAPTER SETUP (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-inference-scale—initial hardware reference values
# │
# │ Goal: Establish H100 and A100 memory/bandwidth for the 'Memory Exhaustion'
# │       section and initial footnotes, plus the recurring 70B FP16/INT4
# │       weight footprints quoted throughout the chapter.
# │ Show: "80" GB, "3.35" TB/s, 140 GB (70B FP16), 35 GB (70B INT4),
# │       26 GB (13B FP16), 500 ms LLM TTFT target.
# │ How: Hardware.Cloud.{H100,A100}; Models.Language.{Llama2_70B,Llama2_13B}
# │      size_in_bytes; Scenarios.ChatbotServing.sla_latency.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_qty_int, fmt_time

class InferenceSetup:
    """Namespace for localized inference hardware reference values."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    mem_h_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity
    bw_h_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth
    bw_a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.bandwidth
    nvlink = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth
    nvlink_per_dir = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth_per_direction
    gpt4 = Models.Language.GPT4
    mem_a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.capacity
    llama70b = Models.Language.Llama2_70B
    llama13b = Models.Language.Llama2_13B
    llm_ttft_slo = Scenarios.ChatbotServing.sla_latency

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_mem = mem_h_h100
    h100_bw = bw_h_h100
    a100_bw = bw_a100
    gpt4_weights_fp16 = gpt4.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    llama70b_fp16 = llama70b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    llama70b_int4 = llama70b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT4)
    llama13b_fp16 = llama13b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(h100_bw > a100_bw, "H100 bandwidth should exceed A100 bandwidth")
    check(abs((nvlink / nvlink_per_dir).to("").magnitude - 2) < 1e-9, "Per-direction NVLink must be half the bidirectional total")
    check(gpt4_weights_fp16 > 40 * h100_mem, "GPT-4-class FP16 weights should dwarf a single H100's HBM")
    check(h100_mem < llama70b_fp16 < 2 * h100_mem, "70B FP16 weights must exceed one 80 GB GPU but fit on two")
    check(llama70b_int4 < mem_a100, "70B INT4 weights must fit on a single A100")
    check(llama13b_fp16 < mem_a100, "13B FP16 weights must fit on a single A100")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(h100_mem, unit=GiB, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_mem_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    a100_mem_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(a100_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    nvlink_h100_per_dir_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink_per_dir, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt4_params_t_str = fmt_params(gpt4.parameters, scale="T", precision=1, commas=False)
    gpt4_weights_tb_str = fmt_memory(gpt4_weights_fp16, unit=TB, precision=1, commas=False, approx=True)
    llama70b_fp16_gb_str = fmt_memory(llama70b_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    llama70b_int4_gb_str = fmt_memory(llama70b_int4, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    llama13b_fp16_gb_str = fmt_memory(llama13b_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    llm_ttft_slo_ms_str = fmt_time(llm_ttft_slo, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
```

A language model that costs millions of dollars to train over two months can, once deployed to a global user base at thousands of queries per second, consume a comparable sum in inference compute every week. Inference is then no longer a temporary batch job. It is a continuous, latency-sensitive service.

Running that continuous service takes more than an efficient steady-state replica. Fleet efficiency characterizes a replica by how close its decode steps come to the bandwidth floor, how long it takes to become ready, and how much of its held time runs at the ideal rate, each averaged over windows of hours to weeks. Serving policy determines how that capacity is shared when requests arrive unevenly and each carries a latency target. A faster decode step supplies a better service rate, but it does not determine how long requests wait to join a batch, which replica receives them, which requests receive scarce cache space, or when the fleet needs another replica. These decisions connect the local execution toolkit to user-visible performance under load.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The serving replica's program and runtime goodput, its bandwidth floor, and the fusion, graph replay, and compilation levers that shape it are established in @sec-performance-engineering.
:::

The service contract makes that distinction measurable. Offered load is the work arriving at the endpoint, including requests the service may reject; admitted load is the work it accepts. A service-level objective (SLO) specifies the required outcome over a measurement window, such as a latency percentile or successful-request fraction. For language models, request rate alone is insufficient because prompt and output lengths determine different amounts of work. Capacity comparisons must therefore hold the request mix and SLO fixed while measuring how much offered work completes successfully within the targets.

An admitted request passes through routing, preprocessing, queueing, batch formation, model execution, and response delivery, crossing between the host CPU and the accelerator twice on the way (@fig-inference-lifecycle). The host manages admission, tokenization, and detokenization, while the GPU executes the prompt prefill pass and iterative KV-cache decode loop. The figure maps noncompute serving overhead against the time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT, the average gap between streamed tokens) latency budgets. For an autoregressive model, prefill processes the prompt and builds cached attention keys and values; decode extends that KV cache as it generates subsequent tokens. Waiting before prefill delays the first token, while competition during decode delays the stream. The scheduler must budget both delays alongside execution time. Batching and cache management govern work within a replica, sharding changes the replica's capacity, and routing and autoscaling distribute demand across replicas.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Prefill's arithmetic-bound regime and decode's bandwidth floor, measured as MBU, are established in @sec-performance-engineering-fleet-efficiency-metric-dff4.
:::

::: {#fig-inference-lifecycle data-explore="original-v2-inference-lifecycle" data-explore-key="vol2:fig-inference-lifecycle" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**End-to-End Inference Pipeline**: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request's latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute." fig-alt="Two regions labeled CPU and GPU. In the CPU region, requests flow down through a load balancer and a tokenizer. Token IDs pass right to a prefill box in the GPU region, which writes to a KV cache box. A decode box reads from and appends to the KV cache, loops on itself, and sends generated token IDs left to a detokenize box that feeds a response stream. :::

Distribution adds placement and coordination decisions to the local serving problem. Load balancing[^fn-load-balancing-inference] must distribute requests across replicas with different amounts of unfinished work and available memory. Request routing must also account for model-specific characteristics: recommendation systems with large sharded embedding tables require different placement strategies than language models that generate responses token by token. When demand changes faster than new replicas can become ready, routing alone cannot restore capacity. Autoscaling, spare capacity, and admission limits must work together to protect the service's latency targets.

[^fn-load-balancing-inference]: **Load balancing for inference**\index{Load balancing!inference}: Request service times can span milliseconds to tens of seconds as models, prompt lengths, and generated outputs vary. Queue-aware routing exposes that remaining work more directly than assignment counts alone.

Training and serving place costs on different timelines. A model version's training expense can be amortized over its deployment, while serving capacity must follow recurring demand. An e-commerce recommendation service, for example, must accommodate peak shopping traffic without paying for an unnecessarily large idle fleet during quiet periods. Both training efficiency and serving efficiency matter, but the serving decision must also account for when requests arrive and how long they can wait. Building such a service requires three linked decisions: when distribution becomes necessary, how the architecture meets latency targets under varying load, and how resource utilization stays high enough that serving cost does not erode the value the model creates. The worked scenarios that follow size these decisions using registry values for real hardware and models alongside labeled scenario assumptions for traffic, prices, and latency budgets, starting with the physical limits that force a service beyond a single machine.

## Limits of Single-Machine Serving {#sec-inference-scale-singlemachine-serving-insufficient-3f13}

A single accelerator fails a production endpoint in three ways: its memory fills before the model weights or caches fit, its throughput saturates below the arriving query rate, or its forward pass runs longer than a request's latency budget. Overcoming those limits requires distributing work across several devices within one machine or across machines over the network. @Tbl-distribution-triggers categorizes these three triggers and their matching distribution strategies, whose necessity depends on the permitted precision, placement, and service contract.

The first signal is memory exhaustion, which occurs when model parameters, key-value caches, or embedding tables exceed single-device capacity. A single NVIDIA H100 GPU provides `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` of HBM3[^fn-hbm3-memory-bandwidth] memory, whereas an illustrative mixture-of-experts model with ~`{python} InferenceSetup.gpt4_params_t_str` parameters requires `{python} InferenceSetup.gpt4_weights_tb_str` for FP16 weights alone. Keeping all those weights resident on accelerators requires multiple devices regardless of request volume; quantization and offloading change that placement constraint. Recommendation systems with trillion-parameter embedding tables face similar constraints. Meta's DLRM architecture[^fn-dlrm-recommendation-scale] stores embedding tables that require multiple terabytes of memory (@sec-appdx-fleet-assumption-provenance records the provenance of the hardware and model constants used throughout this chapter).

[^fn-hbm3-memory-bandwidth]: **HBM3 capacity and bandwidth**\index{HBM3!bandwidth}: The H100 combines `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` of 3D-stacked DRAM with `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_bw_tb_per_s_str` of bandwidth, compared with `{python} InferenceSetup.a100_mem_bw_tb_per_s_str` for HBM2e on the A100. Capacity determines whether model and cache state fit; bandwidth bounds memory-bound decode throughput.

[^fn-dlrm-recommendation-scale]: **DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model)**\index{DLRM!scale}: Meta's 2019 reference architecture combines dense features processed by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) with sparse features represented by embedding lookups [@naumov2019deep]. This separation permits different placement strategies; it does not require embeddings on CPUs and MLPs on GPUs. Production recommendation characterizations show why this structure matters for serving: embedding-heavy recommendation models create memory-access and capacity constraints that differ from dense convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), or large language model (LLM) inference [@gupta2020architectural].

Beyond memory constraints, throughput limitations emerge when request volume exceeds single-machine capacity even with optimal batching. Consider a recommendation system serving 100,000 queries per second with a 10 ms latency budget. If single-machine throughput peaks at 10,000 QPS, no amount of optimization on that machine can satisfy demand. Horizontal scaling\index{Horizontal scaling!inference replicas} across multiple replicas becomes mandatory.

Finally, latency requirements can motivate distribution even when memory is sufficient. A 70-billion parameter model requires approximately `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_fp16_gb_str` of weight memory in FP16, exceeding a single `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` H100-class GPU before KV cache is considered. Quantization or larger-memory hardware can make a single-device configuration feasible, yet its execution time may still exceed the request budget. Sharding the model\index{Model sharding!latency reduction} across multiple GPUs can divide computation and weight traffic, but it adds communication and synchronization. Because sharding shortens compute-bound prefill and bandwidth-bound decode by different amounts, the latency benefit must be measured for each phase against its own target.

| **Constraint** |             **Single-machine limit**             |                          **Example workload**                         |  **Distribution strategy**  |
|:---------------|:------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------:|
| **Memory**     | `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` (H100) | Illustrative MoE (`{python} InferenceSetup.gpt4_weights_tb_str` FP16) | Tensor/pipeline parallelism |
| **Throughput** |                ~10K QPS (vision)                 |                            100K QPS RecSys                            |    Horizontal replication   |
| **Latency**    |           Forward pass $> \text{SLO}$            |         `{python} InferenceSetup.llm_ttft_slo_ms_str` LLM TTFT        |        Model sharding       |

: **Triggers for Distributed Inference**: Each constraint type indicates different distribution strategies. Memory constraints require model sharding; throughput constraints require replication; latency constraints may require either depending on whether the bottleneck is compute or memory bandwidth. {#tbl-distribution-triggers}

Memory, throughput, and latency triggers all become user-visible once an interactive endpoint starts streaming. Time to first token (TTFT)\index{Time to first token}\index{TTFT!time to first token SLO} determines when the user sees a response begin, while time per output token (TPOT)\index{Time per output token}\index{TPOT!time per output token SLO} determines whether the rest of the response arrives at a readable pace. TPOT is the average of the time between tokens (TBT)\index{Time between tokens!definition}\index{TBT!time between tokens}, the gap between successive streamed tokens, which many serving systems report as inter-token latency (ITL). A stream can meet its TPOT target while a single long TBT gap still stalls the reader, so average cadence is stated here as TPOT and per-gap tail targets as TBT. Protecting both first-token delay and stream cadence is why inference reverses many of the optimization priorities from training.

::: {#chk-inference-distribution-strategy-selection .callout-checkpoint title="Distribution strategy selection"}

Verify your understanding of when to move from single-machine to distributed inference:

- [ ] **Shard vs. replicate**: for a 13B model (`{python} InferenceSetup.llama13b_fp16_gb_str` weights) that fits on a single A100, select model sharding or horizontal replication when throughput requirements double.
- [ ] **Latency floor**: for a real-time speech-to-text service where TBT is the primary bottleneck, determine whether data-parallel replication reduces this latency.
- [ ] **Mandatory sharding**: explain why a 175B model requires multiple `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` GPUs when all FP16 weights must remain accelerator-resident, regardless of request volume.
- [ ] **Latency trigger**: identify when a latency target forces distribution and when added network, serialization, coordination, or queuing overhead can erase the benefit.

:::

## SLO Goodput and the Serving Tax {#sec-inference-scale-serving-tax-overhead-distribution-5ef3}

A replica that runs near its hardware limit still wastes its capacity if requests wait so long in queues, network hops, and host processing that responses arrive after the user's deadline. Because a served request counts as useful work only when it meets its latency and quality targets, every stage it crosses spends part of that contract's budget.

### The inversion from training to inference {#sec-inference-scale-fundamental-inversion-training-vs-inference-8834}

A training iteration that takes 2 seconds instead of the usual 1 second slows a run slightly, and faster steps later can still keep the job on schedule. An interactive request that takes 2 seconds against a 100 ms target fails its contract immediately, even if every subsequent request finishes on time. This contrast between training and inference\index{Training!vs. inference requirements} centers on the unit of useful progress. Training evaluates throughput together with convergence over a run; interactive serving evaluates completed requests against quality and latency targets. Offline inference can also prioritize throughput, while training still loses progress to stragglers and stalls. The distinction is therefore which delays violate the workload's contract, not whether one activity cares about time and the other does not. That difference reorders priorities across six system aspects, from the primary metric onward (@tbl-training-inference-inversion).

| **Aspect**              |    **Distributed training**   |      **Distributed inference**       |
|:------------------------|:-----------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|
| **Primary metric**      |   Throughput (samples/hour)   |           Latency (p99 ms)           |
| **Acceptable variance** |             Hours             |             Milliseconds             |
| **State management**    |     Checkpoints (periodic)    |      Session state (continuous)      |
| **Batch formation**     |       Large, controlled       |       Request-driven, variable       |
| **Failure tolerance**   |    Restart from checkpoint    | Redirect if capacity and state allow |
| **Cost structure**      | Fixed duration, variable rate |     Variable duration, fixed SLO     |

: **Training vs. Inference System Requirements**: The fundamental inversion from throughput to latency optimization ripples through system design, state management, batch formation, and failure recovery. {#tbl-training-inference-inversion}

Failure handling follows those different contracts. Training restores a checkpoint and repeats lost work, charging recovery time to the run. Interactive serving has far less time per request, so redirecting work needs spare capacity and recoverable request state, and substituting a smaller model needs an acceptable quality fallback. SLOs\index{SLO!inference latency bounds}\index{SLA!service-level objective} define which failures and delays the service may tolerate, and a recovery mechanism helps only when its added work fits within that contract.

The same targets also define the serving system's capacity metric. **SLO goodput**\index{Goodput!SLO-constrained} is the rate of completed requests that meet the stated TTFT and TPOT targets for a fixed request mix. It is the serving counterpart of the useful-progress goodput that coordination protects in training (@sec-vol2-introduction-dim-coord), and it applies after ML goodput, which measures how much of a replica's held capacity runs at its ideal rate. SLO goodput then counts how much of that capacity completes requests within their targets. A request that misses its contract counts for nothing, however busy the accelerators were while serving it, so increasing arrivals without completing more requests within those targets does not increase useful capacity.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ ML goodput, the fraction of fleet capacity that becomes useful work at the ideal rate, and its three factors are established in @sec-performance-engineering-measurement-scale.
:::

### The serving tax {#sec-inference-scale-serving-tax-budget}

If an interactive request carries a 100 ms latency target and model execution takes 70 ms on an idle replica, routing, network transfers, serialization, coordination, and queueing must all fit inside the remaining 30 ms. Distributing inference adds transfers and coordination to a request that already spends time in host processing and queues. This "serving tax" is the exposed work outside model execution that consumes the request's latency budget, and its size depends on which components the request crosses and which costs can overlap.

Network communication contributes setup and transfer time at each cross-machine dependency. Synchronization between GPUs\index{Synchronization!multi-node latency overhead} can expose that cost when the next operation needs a remote result. For an illustrative path with four sequential exchanges taking 50–500 microseconds each, the exposed contribution is 200 microseconds to 2 milliseconds. Actual collective time also depends on payload, topology, contention, and the number of communication rounds; a generic network round-trip time cannot be charged once per collective without checking its implementation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ model, which splits each transfer into a fixed startup latency plus a bandwidth-dependent term, is established in @sec-network-fabrics-performance-model.
:::

Before and after those network hops, serialization adds host work whenever a service converts structured data into a wire representation and reconstructs it at the receiver. Protocol Buffers, JSON, and Python's `pickle` provide different representations and implementation paths, so their cost must be measured for the actual payload and runtime. Tensor transfers within a sharded model need not pass through the same object-serialization path as a service request. Formats such as FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto\index{Zero-copy!serialization}\index{Serialization!zero-copy} permit access to wire-format data in place, avoiding a separate unpacking step when the consumer supports that representation, though they do not eliminate network transfer or every downstream copy.

Once the payload is on the wire, load balancing adds a routing decision and sometimes another forwarding hop: examining request metadata, consulting replica state, and forwarding to the selected backend all consume time before execution begins. The measurement must separate decision time from waiting and transport so that a slow routing path is not mistaken for a slow model.

When a request fans out across several backend services—such as feature stores, retrieval indexes, and ranking models—coordination overhead emerges as the gateway joins their results. Independent feature or model calls can run concurrently, but a dependent ranking stage must wait for the inputs it needs, so the critical path includes exposed coordination and the slowest required branch rather than the sum of every branch's runtime. Finally, queuing delay ($\QueueingLatency$) adds waiting time whenever work arrives while the required resources are busy, even when the average arrival rate remains below average service capacity.

The serving tax\index{Serving tax!latency breakdown} must be measured on the same request boundary as model execution. @Eq-serving-tax decomposes that latency, with each term counting an exposed contribution so concurrent work is not counted twice:

$$\EndToEndRequestLatency= \InferenceLatency+ \NetworkLatency+ \SerializationLatency+ \CoordinationLatency+ \QueueingLatency$$ {#eq-serving-tax}

In the 100 ms request budget above, the four sequential exchanges alone can claim up to 2 ms of the 30 ms non-compute slack before any request waits for a busy replica. The measured contribution determines the intervention: co-location removes a network hop, fewer dependent exchanges reduce startup costs, and a faster link shortens large transfers, whereas queueing requires controlling admitted work or increasing usable capacity. Each choice spends resources to recover latency budget, connecting the request-level diagnosis to lifetime serving cost.

## Serving Cost Dominance in Production {#sec-inference-scale-serving-cost-dominates-training-cost-576a}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/inference_serving_cost_dominance.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars on a linear scale. A short gray bar shows a training cost of 2 million dollars; a long orange bar shows first-year serving cost of 18.25 million dollars. A bracket between their ends marks the 9.1 times ratio."}

*At this traffic, one year of serving costs about nine times the training run.*
:::

A team that budgets millions of dollars to train a model can find within weeks of launch that serving traffic is spending more compute per month than the entire training run cost. While the serving tax in @eq-serving-tax consumes a fraction of each request's latency budget, those per-request costs compound across every query over the model's operational lifetime. By the serving cost dominance principle\index{Serving cost dominance} (\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}), recurring serving expense\index{Serving cost!upfront vs. recurring expense} can dwarf upfront training expense by orders of magnitude because a model version incurs training cost once before deployment while serving cost recurs with traffic. Both activities can consume purchased or rented infrastructure; the distinction here is expense timing, not financial capitalization. In a high-volume deployment, that recurring traffic bill rapidly overtakes the one-time training investment (notebook \ref{nbk-inference-serving-cost-multiplier}).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: serving-cost-multiplier-simple
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERVING-COST MULTIPLIER (Upfront vs Recurring)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-inference-serving-cost-multiplier worked-example callout —
# │          the "Problem", "Math", and "Systems insight" prose immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compare annual serving expense with training expense for one model version.
# │ Show:    Annual request volume, cost/request, annual serving cost, the
# │          serving/training ratio, and the savings from an efficiency gain.
# │ How:     Scenario assumptions (DAU, reqs/day, cost/request, efficiency gain)
# │          combine with DAYS_PER_YEAR to derive annual volume and cost.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class ServingCostSimple:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    training_cost = 2_000_000  # scenario assumption: one-time training spend
    dau = 1_000_000  # scenario assumption: daily active users
    reqs_per_day = 50  # scenario assumption: requests per user per day
    days_per_year = DAYS_PER_YEAR
    cost_per_request = 0.001  # scenario assumption: serving cost per request
    efficiency_gain = 0.10  # scenario assumption: efficiency improvement
    dau_exp = 6  # 10^6 users, displayed in scientific form
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    annual_reqs = dau * reqs_per_day * days_per_year
    annual_reqs_b = annual_reqs / BILLION
    annual_serving_cost = annual_reqs * cost_per_request
    serving_training_ratio = annual_serving_cost / training_cost
    efficiency_savings = annual_serving_cost * efficiency_gain
    # Scenario B of @fig-serving-cost-crossover: serving spend matches training spend.
    monthly_serving_cost = annual_serving_cost / 12
    crossover_months = training_cost / monthly_serving_cost
    crossover_weeks = crossover_months * days_per_year / 12 / 7
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(annual_reqs > 10e9, "Should be >10B annual requests")
    check(round(serving_training_ratio) == 9, "Serving/training ratio should round to 9x")
    check(round(crossover_weeks) == 6, "Crossover prose says roughly six weeks for the 70B LLM scenario")
    check(10**dau_exp == dau, "dau_exp must match dau in scientific form")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    annual_reqs_calc_math = fmt_math(
        rf"10^{{{dau_exp}}}\,\text{{users}} \times {reqs_per_day}\,\text{{reqs}} " rf"\times {days_per_year}\,\text{{days}} \approx"
    )
    annual_reqs_b_str = fmt_count(annual_reqs, scale="B", precision=2, commas=False)
    annual_serving_cost_str = fmt_usd(annual_serving_cost)
    serving_training_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(serving_training_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
    efficiency_savings_str = fmt_usd(efficiency_savings, precision=1, commas=False, scale="M")
    training_cost_str = fmt_usd(training_cost)
    dau_str = fmt_int(dau)
    reqs_per_day_str = fmt_int(reqs_per_day, commas=False)
    cost_per_request_usd_str = fmt_usd(
        cost_per_request,
        precision=3,
        commas=False,
        per="request",
    )
    efficiency_gain_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(efficiency_gain * 100) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {#nbk-inference-serving-cost-multiplier .callout-notebook title="The serving cost multiplier"}

**Problem**: A team has spent `{python} ServingCostSimple.training_cost_str` training a 70B parameter model and now serves it to `{python} ServingCostSimple.dau_str` daily active users, each making `{python} ServingCostSimple.reqs_per_day_str` requests/day. Is training or serving the dominant cost over 1 year?

**Math**:

1.  **Training cost**\index{Training cost}: `{python} ServingCostSimple.training_cost_str` (one-time).
2.  **Metric**: Annual inference volume is `{python} ServingCostSimple.annual_reqs_calc_math` `{python} ServingCostSimple.annual_reqs_b_str` requests/year.
3.  **Cost per request**\index{Serving cost!cost per request}: Assume a 70B model on H100 costs $\approx$ `{python} ServingCostSimple.cost_per_request_usd_str` (input + output).
4.  **Annual serving cost**\index{Serving cost!annual serving cost}: `{python} ServingCostSimple.annual_reqs_b_str` requests $\times$ `{python} ServingCostSimple.cost_per_request_usd_str` = `{python} ServingCostSimple.annual_serving_cost_str`.

**Systems insight**: Serving costs `{python} ServingCostSimple.serving_training_ratio_mult_str` more than training in the first year alone. A `{python} ServingCostSimple.efficiency_gain_pct_str` reduction in cost per request, at unchanged request volume and service quality, saves about `{python} ServingCostSimple.efficiency_savings_str` in the first year, nearly paying for the original training run.

:::

For one model version at a fixed query rate and average cost per served query, @eq-total-cost combines training expense with recurring serving expense:

$$\ModelLifetimeCost= \TrainingCost + \ServingCostPerQuery\times \DeploymentDuration\times \ArrivalRate$$ {#eq-total-cost}

where $\TrainingCost$ is the one-time cost to train the model, $\ServingCostPerQuery$ is the cost per query served, $\DeploymentDuration$ is the deployment duration in appropriate time units, and $\ArrivalRate$ is the query rate. The rate must count the same served queries used to estimate unit cost. That cost must include the chosen serving boundary, including idle or reserved capacity when it is billed. Changing traffic mix, fleet size, or price requires evaluating separate intervals rather than treating one unit cost as constant throughout deployment.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: inference-economics-refactor
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INFERENCE ECONOMICS AND TCO (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-inference-scale-serving-cost-dominates-training-cost-576a—training vs serving costs
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the dominance of serving cost over training cost.
# │ Show: ~800x leverage for serving optimization in high-traffic RecSys.
# │ How: Lifetime_cost = Traffic * Duration * Cost_per_query.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Infrastructure
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_rate, fmt_usd
from mlsysim.core.units import USD, hour

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class InferenceEconomics:
    """Namespace for inference vs training cost analysis."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Training
    n_gpu_hours = 1000
    cost_per_gpu_hour = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude  # volume price canon
    engineering_multiplier = 3.0

    # Serving
    qps = 10000
    serve_duration_days = 730  # 2 years
    cost_per_query = 1e-5  # $10 per million

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    training_hardware_cost = n_gpu_hours * cost_per_gpu_hour
    training_total_cost = training_hardware_cost * (1 + engineering_multiplier)

    lifetime_queries_val = qps * SEC_PER_DAY * serve_duration_days
    serving_total_cost_val = lifetime_queries_val * cost_per_query

    leverage_ratio = serving_total_cost_val / training_total_cost

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(leverage_ratio > 100, f"Leverage ratio ({leverage_ratio:.1f}) should be > 100x")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # LaTeX-safe form: "6.31e+11" breaks as 6\.31e\+11; use \times 10^{11}.
    # Wrap in fmt_math() so Quarto re-parses the inline {python} substitution
    # through the markdown pipeline; otherwise the literal "$...$" bypasses
    # Pandoc's math parser and renders as raw text.
    if lifetime_queries_val >= 1e9:
        exp = int(math.floor(math.log10(lifetime_queries_val)))
        mantissa = lifetime_queries_val / 10**exp
        lifetime_queries_latex_math = fmt_math(f"{mantissa:.2f} \\times 10^{{{exp}}}")
    else:
        lifetime_queries_latex_math = fmt_math(f"{lifetime_queries_val:,.0f}")
    training_hardware_cost_str = fmt_usd(training_hardware_cost)
    serving_cost_total_str = fmt_usd(serving_total_cost_val)
    training_cost_total_str = fmt_usd(training_total_cost)
    leverage_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(leverage_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
    qps_str = fmt_rate(qps, "QPS")
    serve_duration_days_str = fmt_int(serve_duration_days, commas=False)
    cost_per_million_queries_usd_str = fmt_usd(
        cost_per_query * MILLION,
        commas=False,
        per="million queries",
    )
    n_gpu_hours_str = fmt_count(n_gpu_hours, label="GPU-hour", plural_label="GPU-hours")
    cost_per_gpu_hour_usd_str = fmt_usd(
        cost_per_gpu_hour,
        commas=False,
        per="GPU-hour",
    )
    engineering_mult_str = fmt_multiple(engineering_multiplier, commas=False, precision=0)
```

The same leverage can hold across application categories with different cost structures. In the chapter's illustrative recommendation scenario, a DLRM trained for `{python} InferenceEconomics.training_cost_total_str` (`{python} InferenceEconomics.training_hardware_cost_str` hardware for `{python} InferenceEconomics.n_gpu_hours_str` at `{python} InferenceEconomics.cost_per_gpu_hour_usd_str`, plus `{python} InferenceEconomics.engineering_mult_str` additional engineering cost for data and experimentation) and served at `{python} InferenceEconomics.qps_str` for `{python} InferenceEconomics.serve_duration_days_str` days accumulates `{python} InferenceEconomics.lifetime_queries_latex_math` lifetime queries. At the assumed `{python} InferenceEconomics.cost_per_million_queries_usd_str`, those queries cost `{python} InferenceEconomics.serving_cost_total_str` to serve, producing a `{python} InferenceEconomics.leverage_ratio_mult_str` ratio in this scenario. Other workload envelopes span orders of magnitude in both terms, and the sensitivity ranges in @tbl-cost-ratios are illustrative envelopes rather than market-price estimates.

| **Application**               | **Training cost** | **Annual serving cost** |
|:------------------------------|:------------------|:------------------------|
| **Recommendation (high QPS)** | \$10K--\$100K     | \$1M--\$10M             |
| **Search ranking**            | \$100K--\$1M      | \$10M--\$100M           |
| **LLM API**                   | \$1M--\$100M      | \$10M--\$1B             |
| **Internal analytics**        | \$1K--\$10K       | \$10K--\$100K           |

: **Illustrative Training and Serving Cost Ranges**: Independent sensitivity ranges for training a model version and serving it for a year. A cost ratio requires a paired training-and-serving scenario; it cannot be inferred from matching endpoints of independent ranges. A deployment must substitute measured traffic and a consistent accounting boundary. {#tbl-cost-ratios}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: serving-cost-curve-model
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERVING COST CURVE MODEL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-serving-cost-curve and the paragraph that introduces it.
# │
# │ Goal: Hold the constructed unit-cost curves and the assumed price in one
# │       place so the figure and the prose quote the same crossings.
# │ Show: Daily request volume at which each curve meets the price line.
# │ How: cost(v) = c0 * (v_ref / v)^k; solve cost(v) = price for v.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_math, fmt_usd, sci_latex

class ServingCostCurve:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    price_per_k_tokens = 0.05  # scenario assumption: price per 1,000 tokens (USD)
    volume_ref = 1e6  # scenario assumption: reference daily request volume
    # (cost at volume_ref in USD per 1,000 tokens, scale exponent): constructed curves
    single_gpu = (0.15, 0.30)  # scenario assumption: unbatched single GPU
    multi_gpu = (0.08, 0.45)  # scenario assumption: batched multi-GPU
    optimized = (0.02, 0.55)  # scenario assumption: fully optimized stack

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    # cost(v) = price  =>  v = v_ref * (c0 / price)^(1/k)
    single_cross = volume_ref * (single_gpu[0] / price_per_k_tokens) ** (1 / single_gpu[1])
    multi_cross = volume_ref * (multi_gpu[0] / price_per_k_tokens) ** (1 / multi_gpu[1])
    optimized_cross = volume_ref * (optimized[0] / price_per_k_tokens) ** (1 / optimized[1])

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(optimized_cross < multi_cross < single_cross, "Optimization must move the crossing to lower volume")
    check(1e3 < optimized_cross and single_cross < 1e8, "Crossings must fall inside the plotted volume range")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    price_per_k_tokens_str = fmt_usd(price_per_k_tokens, precision=2, commas=False)
    optimized_cross_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(optimized_cross, precision=0))
    single_cross_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(single_cross, precision=0))
```

A reduction in cost per completed request yields recurring savings only if workload volume and service quality stay fixed; lower latency alone does not reduce billed capacity. Unit cost also changes with daily request volume, as the constructed cost curves of @fig-serving-cost-curve illustrate. Against its assumed price of `{python} ServingCostCurve.price_per_k_tokens_str` per 1,000 tokens, the optimized curve crosses near `{python} ServingCostCurve.optimized_cross_math` requests per day and the unbatched single-GPU curve near `{python} ServingCostCurve.single_cross_math` requests. These crossings follow from the assumed curves, not measured profitability, so a deployment needs its own token mix, occupied capacity, and cost boundary to locate its break-even point.

::: {#fig-serving-cost-curve fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Serving Cost Curve**: Constructed unit-cost curves cross an assumed price line at different request volumes. The optimized curve crosses earlier under these assumptions; the crossings do not establish measured profitability or guaranteed savings from quantization and batching." fig-alt="Log-log plot of cost per 1000 tokens vs. daily request volume for single-GPU, multi-GPU, and optimized serving, drawn as three gray lines that grow heavier with optimization, the optimized line darkest, each labeled at its right end. A dashed horizontal price line divides a shaded region above it, where cost exceeds price, from a shaded region below it, and an open circle marks where each of the three curves crosses the line."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERVING COST CURVE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-serving-cost-curve—inference economics
# │
# │ Goal: Plot cost per 1000 tokens vs daily volume for single-GPU, multi-GPU,
# │       optimized; show break-even vs typical pricing.
# │ Show: Log-log; three curves; break-even line; shaded regions.
# │ How: Power-law cost models; matplotlib.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Plot cost per 1000 tokens vs daily volume for single-GPU, multi-GPU,
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style
import numpy as np

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(5.6, 3.9))
FS = 10.5  # prints at >= 9 pt when the figure is scaled to 5 in

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Curve parameters and the price come from the ServingCostCurve LEGO cell.
volume = np.logspace(3, 8, 200)
typical_pricing = ServingCostCurve.price_per_k_tokens
v_ref = ServingCostCurve.volume_ref

cost_single_gpu = ServingCostCurve.single_gpu[0] * (v_ref / volume) ** ServingCostCurve.single_gpu[1]
cost_multi_gpu = ServingCostCurve.multi_gpu[0] * (v_ref / volume) ** ServingCostCurve.multi_gpu[1]
cost_optimized = ServingCostCurve.optimized[0] * (v_ref / volume) ** ServingCostCurve.optimized[1]

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The three deployments are ordinal (naive -> batched -> optimized), so they
# share one neutral hue at stepped stroke weight; green and red belong only to
# the profit and loss regions. Every stroke is opaque so labels stay legible.
series = (
    (cost_single_gpu, COLORS['secondary'], 1.3, 'Single-GPU\n(naive)'),
    (cost_multi_gpu, COLORS['secondary'], 2.3, 'Multi-GPU\nbatching'),
    (cost_optimized, COLORS['primary'], 2.8, 'Fully\noptimized'),
)
for cost, col, lw, _ in series:
    ax.plot(volume, cost, color=col, linewidth=lw, solid_capstyle='butt')

ax.axhline(y=typical_pricing, color=COLORS['primary'], linestyle='--', linewidth=1.1)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Regions are defined by the price line alone: above it each request loses
# money, below it each request is profitable.
y_lo, y_hi = 1e-3, 3.0
ax.axhspan(typical_pricing, y_hi, color=COLORS['RedL'], alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axhspan(y_lo, typical_pricing, color=COLORS['GreenL'], alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.text(
    1.3e3,
    typical_pricing / 1.2,
    "Typical price\n(break-even)",
    fontsize=FS,
    linespacing=1.05,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['primary'],
    ha='left',
    va='top',
)
ax.text(8e7, 2.3, "cost above price", fontsize=FS, color=COLORS['RedLine'], ha='right', va='top', style='italic')
ax.text(1.3e3, 1.4e-3, "cost below price", fontsize=FS, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], ha='left', va='bottom', style='italic')

# Break-even point of each curve (where it meets the price line) and a
# direct label at the curve's right end in place of a legend.
for cost, col, lw, name in series:
    idx = np.argmax(cost <= typical_pricing)
    if cost[idx] <= typical_pricing:
        ax.plot(volume[idx], typical_pricing, 'o', ms=7, mfc='white', mec=col, mew=2, zorder=5)
    ax.text(volume[-1] * 1.35, cost[-1], name, fontsize=FS, color=col, fontweight='bold', ha='left', va='center', clip_on=False, linespacing=1.0)

ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Daily request volume', fontsize=FS + 0.5)
ax.set_ylabel('Cost per 1,000 tokens ($)', fontsize=FS + 0.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=FS)
ax.set_xlim(1e3, 1e8)
ax.set_ylim(y_lo, y_hi)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.subplots_adjust(right=0.80)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

The cost ranges in @tbl-cost-ratios give a static comparison. @Fig-serving-cost-crossover instead accumulates assumed monthly serving expense over a 36-month deployment and marks when the serving portion equals the initial training expense, within days in the plotted recommendation scenario and roughly six weeks in the 70B LLM scenario. These timings follow from the specified expenses, not from model size or user count, and a larger training expense, lower traffic, or shorter deployment can reverse which activity dominates. When recurring traffic makes inference the dominant expense, serving-specific designs can substantially reduce cost and power per query [@patel2024], provided each optimization targets the workload's actual bottleneck and the right level of the serving stack.

::: {#fig-serving-cost-crossover fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Serving Cost Crossover**: Cumulative total deployment cost (initial training plus ongoing serving) for three illustrative scenarios. Vertical markers (scenarios A and B) indicate when the serving portion equals the one-time training cost. In the two high-traffic scenarios, serving expense matches training expense within weeks or days. In the low-traffic scenario, training expense remains larger over the plotted period. These differences follow from the specified training costs, traffic, and unit serving prices." fig-alt="Line chart on a log cost axis showing cumulative total deployment cost over 36 months for three scenarios, drawn as gray lines of different weights and labeled at their right ends with each scenario's training and monthly serving cost. Dotted horizontal lines mark each scenario's training cost, open circles mark where each total reaches twice its training cost, and for scenarios A and B a short dashed vertical segment rises from the training baseline to that circle."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERVING COST CROSSOVER (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-serving-cost-crossover—training vs serving cost dynamics
# │
# │ Goal: Plot cumulative cost over 36 months for three scenarios; show
# │       crossover where serving overtakes training.
# │ Show: Three lines; fill_between; crossover markers.
# │ How: total_cost = train + serve_per_month*months; vertical markers show
# │      where the serving portion equals the one-time training cost.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Plot cumulative cost over 36 months for three scenarios; show
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(5.6, 4.1))
FS = 10.5  # prints at >= 9 pt when the figure is scaled to 5 in

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
months = np.linspace(0, 36, 500)

# Scenario A: Small model, low traffic
train_a = 0.05  # $50K = $0.05M
serve_per_month_a = 0.005  # $5K/month = $0.005M
cum_a_train = np.full_like(months, train_a)
cum_a_serve = train_a + serve_per_month_a * months
crossover_a = train_a / serve_per_month_a  # 10 months

# Scenario B: 70B LLM, loaded from the ServingCostSimple notebook cell ($M)
train_b = ServingCostSimple.training_cost / MILLION
serve_per_month_b = ServingCostSimple.monthly_serving_cost / MILLION
dau_b_m = ServingCostSimple.dau / MILLION
cum_b_train = np.full_like(months, train_b)
cum_b_serve = train_b + serve_per_month_b * months
crossover_b = ServingCostSimple.crossover_months  # about six weeks

# Scenario C: RecSys, 100M DAU
train_c = 0.012  # $12K = $0.012M
serve_per_month_c = 0.250  # $250K/month = $0.250M
cum_c_train = np.full_like(months, train_c)
cum_c_serve = train_c + serve_per_month_c * months
crossover_c = train_c / serve_per_month_c  # ~0.048 months

# Plot cumulative total cost (training + serving) for each scenario

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Scenarios are categories, not resources: one neutral hue at stepped weight
# (matching the serving cost curve), with direct labels at the right end.
col_a, lw_a = COLORS["secondary"], 1.4
col_b, lw_b = COLORS["primary"], 2.6
col_c, lw_c = COLORS["secondary"], 2.4
# (curve, training cost, crossover month, color, stroke, label, label y, va)
scen = (
    (cum_a_serve, train_a, crossover_a, col_a, lw_a, "A: small model, low traffic\n\\$50K train, \\$5K/mo serve", 0.30, "bottom"),
    (
        cum_b_serve,
        train_b,
        crossover_b,
        col_b,
        lw_b,
        f"B: 70B LLM, {dau_b_m:.0f}M DAU\n\\${train_b:.0f}M train, \\${serve_per_month_b:.1f}M/mo serve",
        70,
        "bottom",
    ),
    (cum_c_serve, train_c, crossover_c, col_c, lw_c, "C: RecSys, 100M DAU\n\\$12K train, \\$250K/mo serve", 10.5, "bottom"),
)
for cum, train, xc, col, lw, name, ly, va in scen:
    ax.plot(months, cum, color=col, linewidth=lw)
    # Training cost baseline (flat dotted line): the gap between a baseline
    # and its curve is the cumulative serving portion.
    ax.axhline(y=train, color=col, alpha=0.8, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.0)
    # Crossover point: total cost = 2 x training cost
    ax.plot(xc, 2 * train, "o", ms=7, mfc="white", mec=col, mew=2, zorder=5, clip_on=False)
    # Direct label inside the plot, beside the curve's right end.
    ax.text(35.6, ly, name, fontsize=FS, color=col, ha="right", va=va, linespacing=1.1)

# Vertical markers for scenarios A and B: a dashed segment from the training
# baseline up to the crossover point, where the serving portion has grown to
# equal the one-time training cost.
for xc, train, col in ((crossover_a, train_a, col_a), (crossover_b, train_b, col_b)):
    ax.plot([xc, xc], [train, 2 * train], color=col, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.annotate(
    f"Crossover: month {crossover_a:.0f}",
    xy=(crossover_a, 2 * train_a),
    fontsize=FS,
    color=col_a,
    fontweight="bold",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    xytext=(12.0, 0.033),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col_a, lw=0.9, shrinkB=5),
)

ax.annotate(
    f"LLM: serving exceeds\ntraining in ~{ServingCostSimple.crossover_weeks:.0f} weeks",
    xy=(crossover_b, 2 * train_b),
    fontsize=FS,
    color=col_b,
    fontweight="bold",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    xytext=(3.0, 110),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col_b, lw=0.9, shrinkB=5),
)

ax.annotate(
    "RecSys: serving dominates within days",
    xy=(crossover_c, 2 * train_c),
    fontsize=FS,
    color=col_c,
    fontweight="bold",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    xytext=(2.2, 0.0072),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col_c, lw=0.9, shrinkB=5),
)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Months since deployment", fontsize=FS + 0.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative cost ($M)", fontsize=FS + 0.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=FS)
ax.set_xlim(-0.8, 36)
ax.set_ylim(0.005, 300)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

## Serving Workloads and the Serving Hierarchy {#sec-inference-scale-serving-hierarchy-fe8c}

An optimization tuned for one model family or one layer of the stack can miss the active bottleneck when applied to another. Paging a key-value cache does nothing for an embedding-heavy recommendation model, and fusing a GPU kernel cannot rescue a service whose requests stall in a load balancer. Controlling serving cost therefore requires separating the workload mix from the system layer that owns each bottleneck.

### Inference beyond LLMs {#sec-inference-scale-inference-landscape-beyond-llms-9560}

Designing a serving platform around autoregressive token generation alone leaves a fleet unprepared for the workloads that dominate consumer request volume. In large consumer platforms, recommendation and ranking workloads\index{Recommendation system!inference traffic volume} can consume the majority of AI inference cycles and capacity [@gupta2020architectural; @hazelwood2018], stalling on terabyte-scale sparse embedding lookups under sub-10 ms deadlines rather than sequential weight reads. Vision and image processing\index{Vision model!serving characteristics}, NLP and LLM workloads, fraud detection, ads, and other classification tasks create additional serving demands. @Tbl-inference-landscape compares representative pressures: sparse lookup for recommendation, batch efficiency for fixed-shape vision, weight and cache traffic for LLM decode, and incremental deadlines for speech. These are starting points for diagnosis; the active bottleneck still depends on the model, input shape, and deployment.

Recommendation traffic illustrates why request volume must be derived from application behavior. A page load, scroll, or click can trigger ranking or retrieval, so one browsing session can produce many inference requests. A language-model application may likewise issue several model calls for one user action or run background tasks without an explicit query. Capacity planning therefore counts the model work triggered by each interaction rather than treating user count as request rate.

Workload structure also determines which techniques can help. Embedding sharding and lookup locality address large recommendation models [@naumov2019deep; @gupta2020architectural], and feature store architectures\index{Feature store!recommendation systems} must deliver the inputs a model expects within its latency budget, while continuous batching and KV cache management address variable-length autoregressive work. Text-to-image systems such as DALL-E add multimodal serving demands [@ramesh2021zero] whose volume and latency targets remain product-specific.

| **Model type**               |        **Serving pressure**       |  **Latency target** |    **Key challenge**     |
|:-----------------------------|:---------------------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------------:|
| **Recommendation/ranking**   | High volume in consumer platforms | $<10\text{ ms}$ p99 |     Embedding lookup     |
| **Vision (CNN)**             |         Workload-dependent        |      20--100 ms     |     Batch efficiency     |
| **LLM**                      |       High cost per request       |     100 ms--10s     |     Memory bandwidth     |
| **Speech/Audio**             |           Stream-driven           |      Real-time      |    Sequential decode     |
| **Multimodal/text-to-image** |   Emerging and product-specific   |        Varies       | Cross-modal coordination |

: **Production Inference Landscape**: Different model types create different serving pressure, latency requirements, and optimization challenges. The table is a qualitative workload map rather than a universal traffic-share distribution. Technique selection must match the specific workload. {#tbl-inference-landscape}

### The serving hierarchy {#sec-inference-scale-serving-hierarchy-levels}

Tuning a replica's kernels or cache allocator cannot fix tail latency when requests are waiting inside a router or starving behind a noisy neighbor on a shared cluster. To locate the right control, serving optimizations organize into a four-level serving hierarchy\index{Serving!hierarchy} ordered by scope, where each level owns a distinct bottleneck and measurement boundary. The request level follows one request through preprocessing, batch-formation waiting, response caching, and model execution, where the target is the latency a user sees. The replica level looks inside one model instance, where utilization, KV-cache memory management, and kernel efficiency set the throughput it can deliver before it saturates. The service level turns many replicas of the same model into aggregate capacity through load balancing, request routing, and autoscaling. The platform level decides, across services and tenants, whether a shared serving fleet stays efficient without allowing one workload to degrade another.

Each level supplies a different measurement boundary. @Tbl-serving-hierarchy associates request latency, replica throughput, aggregate service capacity, and cross-tenant efficiency with the controls most directly responsible for them. Their effects still cross boundaries: batching can increase replica throughput while adding request delay, and replica placement can change both communication cost and service capacity. The hierarchy helps locate the decision without treating its metric in isolation. In C³ terms, batching and cache management improve compute reuse, sharding introduces communication, and routing, isolation, and autoscaling coordinate the resources that make those gains usable.

| **Level**    | **Optimization target** | **Key techniques**                   |
|:-------------|:-----------------------:|:-------------------------------------|
| **Request**  |   Per-request latency   | Dynamic batching, response caching   |
| **Replica**  | Throughput, utilization | KV-cache paging, kernel fusion       |
| **Service**  |    Aggregate capacity   | Load balancing, routing, autoscaling |
| **Platform** |   Resource efficiency   | Multi-tenancy, scheduling, placement |

: **Serving Hierarchy Optimization Targets**: Each level of the serving hierarchy targets distinct performance metrics, from per-request latency at the request tier to aggregate resource efficiency at the platform tier. {#tbl-serving-hierarchy}

::: {#chk-inference-serving-hierarchy .callout-checkpoint title="The serving hierarchy"}

Verify your understanding of where specific optimizations sit within the serving hierarchy:

- [ ] **Replica level**: identify the hierarchy level at which KV-cache paging reduces GPU memory waste, and explain why that raises concurrent request capacity rather than single-request latency.
- [ ] **Caching level**: distinguish response caching, which shortens one request's path, from KV-cache paging, which raises a replica's capacity, and place each in the hierarchy.
- [ ] **Load balancing**: identify why load balancing belongs at the service level and explain how its choice of replica can affect both aggregate goodput and a request's queueing delay.
- [ ] **Isolation level**: evaluate the claim that multi-tenancy and resource isolation are primarily request-level concerns.

:::

The serving decisions that follow climb the hierarchy from the request level to the platform level. Batching sets how long each request waits to share execution. KV-cache layout, decode-time policies, and adapter state decide how many requests a replica can hold. The split between prefill and decode decides whether a new prompt and the streams already decoding share a worker or separate pools. Weight quantization and model sharding change the replica's memory and compute budget. Routing, isolation, autoscaling, and global placement then turn replicas into a service and a platform. Precision enters every capacity calculation that follows through two separate budgets: reducing weight precision frees resident memory, whereas reducing KV precision lowers the memory required per active sequence. @Sec-inference-scale-weight-quantization-serving-097b compares the serving trade-offs of these representation choices before sharding divides a replica across devices.

## Batching Strategies at Scale {#sec-inference-scale-batching-strategies-scale-6733}

A stream of hundreds of disparate chat requests arrives at an inference server every second. Processing them one by one leaves much of the GPU idle, starved for work between small decode steps. Waiting to gather a large static batch forces the first request in line to endure unacceptable latency. Batching at scale therefore needs policies that group requests as they arrive without violating tail-latency deadlines.

Processing multiple requests together shares weight reads and kernel launch overhead across more useful work. The resulting service-rate gain can reduce queueing, but waiting to form a batch adds delay; the net effect on request latency depends on load. Single-machine serving applies this insight through dynamic batching\index{Dynamic batching}, which collects requests within a time window before processing them together.

At scale, batching must also account for workload structure. A policy suited to uniform vision inputs can leave slots unused during variable-length generation, while grouping sparse embedding lookups solves a different problem from batching dense execution. The unit of reusable work determines which policy is worth evaluating. The strategies below proceed in order of mechanism rather than traffic share: vision (request batching), LLMs (iteration-level batching with KV state), and recommendation (feature-parallel batching over distributed embeddings), even though recommendation often dominates consumer inference volume (@sec-inference-scale-inference-landscape-beyond-llms-9560).

### Batching across model architectures {#sec-inference-scale-batching-differs-across-model-types-2026}

Holding arriving requests until a fixed batch fills forces early arrivals to wait and pads shorter inputs with wasted work, whereas running every request immediately leaves later arrivals queued behind one-request passes that underuse the GPU. Batching efficiency depends on how computation scales with batch size relative to memory and communication constraints, and the execution timeline in @fig-batching-strategies separates waiting to form a batch from waiting for the accelerator to become available. Unbatched serving adds no batch-formation delay, but later requests can still queue behind earlier forward passes. Static batching consolidates all four illustrated requests into one pass, adding formation delay and padding to accommodate different input lengths. Dynamic batching closes formation windows at fixed time intervals ($\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$), producing two passes with two requests each in this example. The window limits intentional formation delay; it does not bound total queueing when ready batches arrive faster than the server can execute them.

::: {#fig-batching-strategies fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Batching Strategies Compared**: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay." fig-alt="Three stacked timelines labeled (a) no batching, (b) static batching, and (c) dynamic batching. Each shows four request rows R1 to R4 with arrival ticks, gray wait segments, blue forward-pass segments, and hatched padding, above a GPU row. The GPU row shows four single-request passes in (a), one four-request pass in (b), and two two-request passes in (c). Dashed violet lines mark when each batch is dispatched."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: memory-wall-ratios
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ACCELERATOR COMPUTE VS. BANDWIDTH GROWTH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: decode-phase paragraph and @fig-gpu-memory-wall caption.
# │
# │ Goal: State how much faster peak compute grew than memory bandwidth from
# │       the first to the last accelerator generation in the figure.
# │ Show: ~18x peak compute vs ~8.9x memory bandwidth (V100 to B200).
# │ How: Ratios of last to first row of data/gpu_memory_wall.csv, the vendor
# │      datasheet values the figure plots.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import csv
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_multiple

class MemoryWallRatios:
    """Peak-compute and bandwidth growth across the plotted accelerator generations."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    with open("vol2/10_inference/data/gpu_memory_wall.csv") as _f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(_f))

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    first, last = rows[0], rows[-1]
    compute_ratio = float(last["Peak_TFLOPS"]) / float(first["Peak_TFLOPS"])
    bandwidth_ratio = float(last["Memory_Bandwidth_GBps"]) / float(first["Memory_Bandwidth_GBps"])

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(compute_ratio > 1.5 * bandwidth_ratio, "Prose says compute outgrew bandwidth by a wide margin")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    compute_mult_str = fmt_multiple(compute_ratio, precision=0, commas=False)
    bandwidth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bandwidth_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
```

In vision models\index{Vision model} processing fixed-size images, arithmetic work grows roughly in proportion to batch size while requests share the weights, so larger batches improve weight reuse until compute, memory, or the latency budget binds. The largest feasible batch is not necessarily the best interactive operating point. By contrast, in LLMs during the decode phase\index{Decode phase!memory bandwidth bound}, small batches perform little computation per byte of active weights loaded, so memory bandwidth binds. Larger batches raise arithmetic intensity until compute, KV-cache traffic, or the latency budget limits further gains. Small-batch decode therefore does not inherit a new accelerator generation's headline compute improvement. From Volta to Blackwell, peak compute climbs `{python} MemoryWallRatios.compute_mult_str` while memory bandwidth expands by only `{python} MemoryWallRatios.bandwidth_mult_str`, and @fig-gpu-memory-wall shows generation throughput tracking the slower curve whenever weight streaming dominates at small batch sizes.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The accelerator trajectory behind this divergence, with compute outpacing memory bandwidth from one generation to the next, is established in @sec-compute-infrastructure-evolution-gpu-architectures-566b.
:::

Recommendation systems shift the bottleneck again: sparse embedding lookup\index{Recommendation system!embedding lookup bottleneck} can limit throughput before dense computation does. Grouping sparse accesses improves locality and distributes lookup work across shards, while batching the dense stages improves matrix multiplication throughput. The serving policy must therefore account for both stages and the communication between them rather than infer the bottleneck from the model category alone.

::: {#fig-gpu-memory-wall fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Decode Inherits the Bandwidth Deficit**: Peak compute and memory bandwidth for four accelerator generations, normalized to the V100. Compute rises `{python} MemoryWallRatios.compute_mult_str` against bandwidth's `{python} MemoryWallRatios.bandwidth_mult_str`. In weight-bandwidth-bound decode, each iteration loads the active weights and reuses them across its output tokens; at fixed batch size, bandwidth growth constrains the gain. These hardware ratios are not measured workload speedups. Specifications are dense peak rates and bandwidths from the vendor datasheets recorded in the chapter's data file." fig-alt="Line chart normalized to the V100 across V100, A100, H100, and B200, showing peak compute reaching 18 times and memory bandwidth 8.9 times by the B200, with the widening gap between the two lines shaded and labeled bandwidth deficit."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

data = pd.read_csv("vol2/10_inference/data/gpu_memory_wall.csv")
base = data.iloc[0]
data["Compute"] = data["Peak_TFLOPS"] / base["Peak_TFLOPS"]
data["Bandwidth"] = data["Memory_Bandwidth_GBps"] / base["Memory_Bandwidth_GBps"]

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(5.6, 3.7))
FS = 10.5  # prints at >= 9 pt when the figure is scaled to 5 in
labels = data["Accelerator"] + "\n" + data["Year"].astype(str)
x = range(len(data))
# The widening gap between the two curves is the bandwidth deficit decode
# inherits. It is a gap, not a failure, so it takes a neutral gray wash (red is
# reserved for danger, orange means compute). Compute is the reference series
# (dark neutral); memory bandwidth is a GB/s quantity, so it takes violet.
ax.fill_between(x, data["Bandwidth"], data["Compute"], color=COLORS["grid"], alpha=0.45, lw=0)
ax.plot(x, data["Compute"], marker="o", color=COLORS["primary"], linewidth=2.2)
ax.plot(x, data["Bandwidth"], marker="s", color=COLORS["VioletLine"], linewidth=2.6)

def _mult(v):
    return f"{v:.1f}".rstrip("0").rstrip(".") + "×"

last = len(data) - 1
for col, name, colour in [("Compute", "Peak compute", COLORS["primary"]), ("Bandwidth", "Memory\nbandwidth", COLORS["VioletLine"])]:
    ax.annotate(
        f"{name}\n{_mult(data[col].iloc[-1])}",
        xy=(last, data[col].iloc[-1]),
        xytext=(9, 0),
        textcoords="offset points",
        va="center",
        ha="left",
        fontweight="bold",
        fontsize=FS,
        color=colour,
        linespacing=1.05,
    )
# Placed inside the widest part of the wedge, clear of both lines.
gap_x = last - 0.41
gap_y = 0.515 * data["Compute"].iloc[-1]
ax.text(gap_x, gap_y, "bandwidth\ndeficit", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=FS, style="italic", color=COLORS["secondary"])

ax.set_xticks(list(x))
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=FS)
ax.set_ylabel(f'Growth relative to {base["Accelerator"]} ({int(base["Year"])})', fontsize=FS + 0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("NVIDIA data center accelerator", fontsize=FS + 0.5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, last + 1.25)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.12 * data["Compute"].max())
fig.tight_layout()
```
