:::

The disaggregation decision therefore depends on a quantitative contract, not on the phase labels alone. If prefill produces $\KvCacheMemory$ bytes of attention state and the usable inter-pool bandwidth is $\LinkBandwidth$, then the handoff consumes at least

$$\KvCacheHandoffTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\KvCacheMemory}{\LinkBandwidth},$$ {#eq-prefill-decode-handoff}

where $\MessageStartupLatency$ includes transfer setup and queueing for the operating point being evaluated; it is not a fixed network latency once load changes. The payload term sets the scale. A 128K-token request on the GQA model of notebook \ref{nbk-inference-kv-cache-capacity-estimator} carries tens of gigabytes of KV state, so moving it over a single `{python} InferenceSetup.nvlink_h100_per_dir_gb_per_s_str` NVLink direction takes on the order of a hundred milliseconds, and an inter-node link takes longer still. Spreading the transfer across a tensor-parallel group divides that time only when each device has its own path to its counterpart in the decode pool. Because $\KvCacheMemory$ grows linearly with prompt length, the long prompts that make disaggregation attractive are also the prompts whose handoff costs most, and that cost lands on TTFT.

@Eq-prefill-decode-handoff therefore makes placement part of the service contract. The prefill pool must sustain the admitted prompt-token rate, the decode pool must sustain the admitted output-token rate, and both pools need headroom for the request-length distribution. Disaggregation justifies its KV-cache transfer cost only when eliminating phase interference and balancing the two pools raises SLO goodput. Otherwise, colocated chunked prefill avoids the additional handoff and pool coordination.

Whether the phases share a worker or split into pools, the base weights remain the largest fixed claim on each device's memory and, for decode, the largest share of the bytes streamed per step. Weight quantization addresses that part of the budget, with numerical quality and execution cost determining how much of the storage saving becomes useful serving capacity.

## Weight Quantization for Serving {#sec-inference-scale-weight-quantization-serving-097b}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/inference_quantization_capacity_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Linear memory ladder comparing a 140 GB FP16 70B model with a 35 GB INT4 70B model. A dashed red vertical line marks one GPU's 80 GB capacity: the FP16 bar crosses it and the INT4 bar ends well inside it. A bracket marks the 4 times reduction."}

*INT4 turns a two-GPU model into a one-GPU candidate.*
:::

Keeping a 70B model's `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_fp16_gb_str` of FP16 weights intact forces every replica across at least two `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` GPUs and makes every decode step wait on streaming `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_fp16_gb_str` from HBM. Weight quantization for serving is therefore a bottleneck-selection decision: reducing precision turns that `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_fp16_gb_str` FP16 weight payload into a `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_int4_gb_str` INT4 payload, allowing a model that previously required multiple GPUs to fit on one (perspective \ref{psp-inference-quantization-serving-constraint}). The ideal payload reduction is 4$\times$, although metadata, runtime buffers, and KV state still enter the deployment's memory budget. Because neither quality loss nor speedup is fixed by nominal bit width, both must be measured for the deployed representation and workload.

::: {#psp-inference-quantization-serving-constraint .callout-perspective title="Quantization as a serving constraint"}

In serving systems, quantization changes the binding resource as well as the model's size. Post-training quantization\index{Post-training quantization!calibration} (PTQ) can shrink a deployed model without retraining, while quantization-aware training\index{Quantization-aware training!simulated rounding error} (QAT) spends training effort to preserve accuracy at lower precision. QAT simulates low-precision rounding in the forward pass and passes gradients through the rounding step as if it were absent, the straight-through estimator [@bengio2013estimating], so the weights adapt to the error they will carry. It earns that cost only after a PTQ recipe misses the quality budget at the target precision, and a recipe that passes at INT8 says nothing about INT4. The practical order is to deploy with PTQ when it meets quality and reach for QAT, or adapter-based fine-tuning of a quantized base, when it does not, rechecking quality after the final deployment conversion. The systems question is which constraint the lower-precision representation relaxes: GPU memory capacity, HBM bandwidth during decode, accelerator instruction support, or cost per served token.

:::

Choosing a quantized representation starts with deciding which quantity should shrink: resident weights for fit, bytes moved per decode step for bandwidth, activations for prefill throughput, or the precision path supported by target hardware. Serving at scale also introduces distinct operational constraints: a deployment team may need post-training quantization without the original training corpus, quality must be preserved across diverse inputs, and hardware deployment targets vary from data center GPUs to edge accelerators. Lack of the original corpus does not imply data-free calibration; the methods that follow may still require representative deployment inputs. Production inference therefore starts from a decision model rather than from the methods. @Tbl-serving-quantization-decision-model ties each method family to the serving constraint it relaxes; what changes for each when it is deployed is its calibration cost, kernel path, and the evaluation a serving team must run.

| **Binding serving constraint** | **Representation change**                       | **Method family**       | **Risk to test before rollout**             |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Model does not fit in memory   | Quantize weights only                           | GPTQ, AWQ               | Calibration mismatch and quality regression |
| Decode is bandwidth-bound      | Reduce bytes read per token                     | W4A16 weight-only paths | Kernel support and KV-cache headroom        |
| Prefill is compute-bound       | Quantize weights and activations                | SmoothQuant W8A8        | Activation outliers and INT8 hardware path  |
| Outliers block low precision   | Change the coordinate basis before quantization | Rotation-based methods  | Transform overhead and limited runtime path |

: **Serving Quantization Decision Model**: Quantization methods are useful only when they relax the resource that binds the serving system. The method family follows from the bottleneck: fit, bandwidth, prefill compute, or outlier robustness. {#tbl-serving-quantization-decision-model tbl-colwidths="[24,28,22,26]"}

### Outliers and block-wise scaling {#sec-inference-scale-block-wise-scaling}

When a single weight or activation channel is ten times larger than its neighbors, uniform per-tensor quantization must either clip that extreme value or stretch its step size across the entire range, collapsing the surrounding small values to zero. Large language models produce such outlier features\index{Outlier feature!quantization challenge} routinely: in the models studied by @dettmers2022llmint8, about 0.1 percent of hidden dimensions\index{Outlier feature!activation magnitude} carried activation magnitudes roughly 3--20$\times$ larger than the rest. Weight tensors face the same damage when a few large weights set the scale for the whole matrix. Block-wise quantization contains that weight-side damage inside the stored format.

::: {#dfn-inference-block-wise-quantization .callout-definition title="Block-wise quantization"}

***Block-wise quantization***\index{Block-wise quantization!definition}\index{Quantization!block-wise} is an ML quantization scheme that partitions a weight tensor into nonoverlapping groups of $\QuantizationBlockSize$ elements and assigns each group its own scale. An affine scheme uses $\QuantizationScale_i = (\BlockRangeMaximum- \BlockRangeMinimum) / (2^\NumericBitWidth- 1)$ together with an offset or zero point; a symmetric scheme centers the range at zero and needs only scale metadata. The metadata examples below assume symmetric scale-only quantization.

1.  **Significance**: With block size $\QuantizationBlockSize = 64$ and $\NumericBitWidth= 4$ bits, weights compress from 16 bits to 4 bits (a 4$\times$ memory reduction) while each FP16 scale adds $16/64 = 0.25$ bits per weight. This yields an effective bit-width of $4.25$ bits per weight: 6.25 percent overhead relative to the INT4 payload, or about 1.6 percent of the original FP16 weight size.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike per-tensor quantization\index{Quantization!per-tensor}, which applies a single scale across the entire weight matrix, block-wise quantization contains outlier damage within individual blocks. Per-tensor scaling forces that scale to accommodate outlier values, which wastes precision on the majority of near-zero weights. A single extreme value therefore cannot degrade quantization fidelity for the whole tensor.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that block size is a free hyperparameter. Smaller blocks ($\QuantizationBlockSize = 32$) can improve local range resolution but double the scale metadata overhead vs. $\QuantizationBlockSize = 64$. At $\QuantizationBlockSize = 16$, the scale adds 1 bit per weight: 25 percent overhead relative to the INT4 payload, or 6.25 percent of the original FP16 weight size. The effect on model quality and kernel speed must be evaluated rather than inferred from block size alone.

:::

The metadata price stays small across formats\index{Block-wise quantization!storage overhead}. An INT8 scheme with one FP32 scale per 128 weights adds $32/128 = 0.25$ bits per weight, about 3 percent of its payload. Block-wise scaling therefore isolates outliers without the bandwidth penalty of a higher-precision format, which keeps the decode traffic saving of a low-bit format intact. @Fig-block-quantization isolates this dynamic-range protection across an eight-weight sample containing a single outlier ($58.7$). Under per-tensor scaling (left), the outlier dictates a coarse scale factor ($\QuantizationScale\approx 0.462$) that forces six of the seven small weights to round to zero. Partitioning the tensor into four-element blocks (right) confines that coarse scale to the second block, allowing the uncorrupted first block to adopt a fine scale ($\QuantizationScale_1 \approx 0.00165$) that preserves full INT8 resolution.

::: {#fig-block-quantization fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block-Wise versus Per-Tensor Quantization**: Under per-tensor scaling (left), one outlier weight sets the scale for the whole tensor, so six of the seven small weights round to zero and the seventh rounds to one. Under block-wise quantization (right), each group of weights gets its own scale: the block without the outlier keeps full INT8 resolution, while the small weights that share the outlier's block are still crushed. Smaller blocks confine the damage further at the cost of more scale metadata." fig-alt="Two side-by-side panels quantize the same eight FP16 weights, one of which is an outlier of 58.7. Left, per-tensor: a single scale of about 0.462 maps six weights to 0, one to 1, and the outlier to 127, with the collapsed cells shaded red. Right, block-wise with blocks of four outlined by dashed boxes: the first block's scale of about 0.00165 maps its weights to 73, -48, 127, and -91, shaded green, while the second block, containing the outlier, maps to 127, 0, 1, and 0."}
![](images/svg/block-quantization.svg)

:::

### LLM-specific quantization challenges {#sec-inference-scale-llmspecific-quantization-challenges-b7a2}

Block-wise scaling handles weight outliers inside the stored format. The outlier activation problem\index{Activation outliers!quantization degradation} is harder, because activations arrive at run time and their extreme channels cannot be rescaled offline block by block. A coarse scale loses resolution for smaller values, while a narrow range clips large ones. This trade-off is not unique to language models, but its channel structure motivates the methods below.

For a serving deployment the consequence is that no single INT8 scale suits both the outlier channels and the typical values. The method families therefore differ in which part of the serving contract they protect, at which stage they pay for it, and what they cost to deploy. LLM.int8()\index{LLM.int8()!mixed-precision decomposition} [@dettmers2022llmint8] pays at run time. It detects outlier dimensions against a magnitude threshold, multiplies them in FP16 and the rest in INT8, and sums the two products. This preserves quality at the cost of outlier detection and a second execution path on every step.

GPTQ\index{GPTQ!layer-by-layer quantization}\index{GPTQ!second-order error compensation} [@frantar2023gptq] and AWQ\index{AWQ!salient weight protection}\index{AWQ!activation-aware scaling} [@lin2023awq] pay offline and both produce 4-bit weight-only artifacts. GPTQ quantizes a layer's weights in sequence and adjusts the still-unquantized weights to compensate for the error already introduced, guided by a second-order estimate from calibration activations of how sensitive the layer's output is to each weight. AWQ instead protects the salient weights, those that multiply large activations, because a small rounding error on a weight channel that multiplies a large activation produces a large output error. Multiplying those salient weight channels by a scale factor greater than one before group quantization forces them to span a larger portion of the shared 4-bit integer grid, reducing their relative rounding error while an inverse scale is applied to the corresponding input activations. Both methods need representative calibration inputs and supported packing kernels, a reconstruction objective that is only a proxy for task quality, and a comparison at the same model, bit budget, and held-out evaluation. AWQ also needs its inverse scales fused into the preceding layer of the deployed graph, or it spends part of the latency saving on an extra runtime operation.

SmoothQuant\index{SmoothQuant!activation-to-weight scaling}\index{SmoothQuant!per-channel scaling} [@xiao2023smoothquant] targets low-precision matrix multiplication rather than weight-only storage and pays in a preprocessing transform. It divides each activation channel by a smoothing factor and multiplies the matching weights by the same factor. This leaves the product unchanged before rounding and migrates part of the extreme activation range into the weights, so that both tensors can fit inside INT8 for W8A8 execution. That matters for compute-bound prefill, although shrinking the activation range stretches the weight range and makes the weights harder to quantize. The smoothing factor therefore balances the two quantization errors, and production activation extremes can still differ from the calibration ranges. Rotation-based methods such as QuaRot\index{Quantization!rotation-based}\index{QuaRot!rotation-based quantization} [@ashkboos2024quarot] apply orthogonal Hadamard transforms that spread large coordinates across channels, which makes W4A4 a serving candidate at the price of some online rotation work.

None of these properties fixes quality. Each artifact must be compared with the FP16 baseline on the same model, evaluation data, and runtime, reporting its calibration set, group size, kernel path, and any online-transform overhead. Its serving benefit must also be measured as SLO-compliant throughput on the target workload rather than inferred from nominal bit width.

### W8A8 versus weight-only ceilings {#sec-inference-scale-smoothquant-migrating-quantization-difficulty-f37f}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: w8a8-ceilings
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ W8A8 VS WEIGHT-ONLY CEILINGS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-smoothquant-w8a8 and the prefill/decode paragraph after it.
# │
# │ Goal: Bound what 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations can buy in each phase.
# │ Show: 2x weight-byte reduction for both schemes; 2x INT8/FP16 peak ratio
# │       on the H100 as the prefill ceiling for W8A8 only.
# │ How: bytes per weight ratio; Hardware.Cloud.H100 int8 vs dense FP16 peak.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_multiple

class W8A8Ceilings:
    """Upper bounds, not measured speedups, for 8-bit serving paths."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    fp16_peak = h100.compute.peak_flops
    int8_peak = h100.compute.precision_flops["int8"]

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_byte_ratio = (BYTES_FP16 / BYTES_INT8).magnitude
    int8_compute_ratio = int8_peak.magnitude / fp16_peak.magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(weight_byte_ratio - 2) < 1e-9, "8-bit weights halve FP16 weight bytes")
    check(1.9 < int8_compute_ratio < 2.1, "INT8 peak should be about twice dense FP16 peak")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(weight_byte_ratio, precision=0, commas=False)
    int8_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(int8_compute_ratio), precision=0, commas=False)
```

Quantizing only the weights (W8A16 or W4A16) cuts weight traffic during decode but leaves compute-bound prefill executing on FP16 Tensor Cores at unchanged arithmetic speed, whereas quantizing both weights and activations (W8A8) risks accuracy loss from activation outliers without further shrinking weight bytes. The prefill-decode split therefore decides which path can pay: both schemes shrink the weights, but only W8A8 changes the arithmetic ceiling. @Tbl-smoothquant-w8a8 bounds what each 8-bit path can buy relative to the FP16 baseline.

| **Configuration**        |                    **Weight bytes**                   |                      **Prefill compute ceiling**                      |          **Decode weight-traffic ceiling**          |   **Quality**    |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------:|:----------------:|
| **FP16 (baseline)**      |                       1$\times$                       |                               1$\times$                               |                      1$\times$                      |     Baseline     |
| **W8A16 (weights only)** | Reduced `{python} W8A8Ceilings.weight_ratio_mult_str` |                         1$\times$ (FP16 math)                         | Up to `{python} W8A8Ceilings.weight_ratio_mult_str` | Measure vs. FP16 |
| **W8A8 (SmoothQuant)**   | Reduced `{python} W8A8Ceilings.weight_ratio_mult_str` | Up to `{python} W8A8Ceilings.int8_ratio_mult_str` (INT8 Tensor Cores) | Up to `{python} W8A8Ceilings.weight_ratio_mult_str` | Measure vs. FP16 |

: **W8A8 SmoothQuant vs. Weight-Only Quantization**: Ceilings derived from bytes per weight and the H100's INT8-to-FP16 peak ratio, not measured speedups. Both schemes halve weight bytes, so both can at most halve weight traffic in bandwidth-bound decode. Only W8A8 moves prefill onto INT8 Tensor Cores. Realized gains and quality loss depend on kernels, calibration, and the request mix. {#tbl-smoothquant-w8a8}

The distinction is which ceiling binds. Among these configurations, W8A8 enables INT8 matrix multiplication, with the illustrated `{python} W8A8Ceilings.int8_ratio_mult_str` peak ratio providing a compute ceiling rather than a measured prefill speedup. Both quantized schemes halve the weight payload. If weight reads dominate decode, activation quantization does not further reduce that traffic, although it can change other memory and compute costs. Quantization and dequantization also add work. The end-to-end benefit therefore depends on the prompt/output mix, batch sizes, and measured execution path.

Hardware and software support decide which of these savings reach the serving workload\index{Quantization!hardware-software co-design}, because the arithmetic format and the resident storage format need not be identical. A common INT4 weight-only kernel reads packed weights and dequantizes them to FP16 on chip during the GEMM, so it cuts weight capacity and read traffic\index{Quantization!weight-only} without any INT4 arithmetic. For batch-one decode dominated by weight reads, throughput then scales roughly as memory bandwidth divided by the model's weight bytes, omitting KV-cache traffic and execution overhead, and leaving the arithmetic in FP16 costs little because arithmetic is not the binding term. At large batch or in prefill, where execution approaches the compute ceiling, the gain comes instead from a weight-activation format, W8A8 or FP8 on hardware with FP8 Tensor Cores\index{Quantization!FP8 formats}, which raises the ceiling that weight-only formats cannot move. In the ideal memory-bound case, 4-bit weights cut weight traffic by 4$\times$, but realized decode throughput depends on kernel support, dequantization overhead, KV-cache precision, batch shape, and whether HBM bandwidth is truly the bottleneck. A serving system can therefore run different formats at different operating points, with each configuration evaluated against the same quality criterion and its own latency targets, and the value of 4-bit serving is strongest when it increases model residency or batch capacity.

### Runtime contract for quantized serving {#sec-inference-scale-framework-integration-945c}

Loading a 4-bit checkpoint into a serving runtime that expands the weights back into resident FP16 tensors at startup or falls back to unoptimized kernels forfeits both the memory capacity and the HBM bandwidth savings before a single request arrives. Production serving frameworks\index{Serving framework!runtime contract} determine whether a quantized artifact retains its intended advantages by converting packed weights inside the execution kernel rather than in HBM. The serving stack must therefore report the resident representation and kernel path, budget KV state around actual allocations, and expose quality and latency regressions (@tbl-quantized-serving-runtime-contract).

| **Runtime responsibility**              | **Why it matters**                                                                       |
|:----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Preserve the quantized artifact         | Full-model expansion into resident FP16 forfeits the reduced weight storage and traffic. |
| Select compatible low-precision kernels | Unsupported operators fall back to slower or higher-precision execution.                 |
| Plan memory around weights and KV cache | The capacity gain matters only if the freed memory becomes useful batch headroom.        |
| Validate quality and latency together   | A lower-bit path that meets latency but fails task quality is not a serving win.         |

: **Quantized Serving Runtime Contract**: Framework-specific APIs differ, but every production path has to preserve representation, choose supported kernels, plan memory, and validate quality under the deployed traffic mix. {#tbl-quantized-serving-runtime-contract tbl-colwidths="[34,66]"}

Weight quantization reduces the weight allocation, while PagedAttention reduces waste in allocating KV state. Both feed the same admission budget as the capacity estimator of notebook \ref{nbk-inference-kv-cache-capacity-estimator}, with quantized weights in place of FP16 ones. That estimate is optimistic, because a usable integer limit must round down after reserving runtime buffers, quantization metadata, and safety headroom, and sharded deployments must satisfy the budget on every device.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: quantized-serving-capacity
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ QUANTIZED SERVING CAPACITY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Quantization + PagedAttention" prose in §Framework integration.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute A100 KV headroom after 4-bit weight quantization and estimate
# │       the number of 1K-token MHA-baseline sequences it can hold.
# │ Show: 80 GB A100, 35 GB weights, 45 GB KV headroom, ~2.6 GB per 1K sequence.
# │ How: 70B * 0.5 bytes for INT4 weights; KV from KVCacheCalc normalized to 1K.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_qty_int

class QuantizedServingCapacity:
    """Estimate single-A100 batch capacity after 4-bit weight quantization."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # nameplate magnitude in decimal GB: the prose subtracts a decimal
    # 35 GB weight from this budget, so both must share a unit space
    a100_mem = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.capacity.to(GiB).magnitude * GB
    a100_kv_budget = a100_mem  # scenario capacity budget
    llama70b = Models.Language.Llama2_70B
    gpt3 = Models.Language.GPT3  # 175B dense reference model
    h100_mem = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_int4 = llama70b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT4)
    gpt3_int4 = gpt3.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT4)
    kv_headroom = a100_kv_budget - weight_int4
    kv_layers = llama70b.layers
    kv_heads = llama70b.heads  # MHA baseline, as in KVCacheCalc
    kv_head_dim = llama70b.hidden_dim // llama70b.heads
    kv_seq_len = int(ReferenceStats.ServingProfiles.PrecisionDividendContextLengthTokens)
    kv_fp16 = calc_kv_cache_size(kv_layers, kv_heads, kv_head_dim, kv_seq_len, 1, BYTES_FP16)
    kv_per_1k_sequence = kv_fp16 / (kv_seq_len / THOUSAND)
    max_1k_sequences = int((kv_headroom / kv_per_1k_sequence).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs((weight_int4 - 35 * GB).to(GB).magnitude) < 1e-9, "70B INT4 weights should be 35 GB")
    check(max_1k_sequences > 10, "Quantized model should leave room for multiple 1K sequences")
    check(gpt3_int4 > h100_mem, "175B INT4 weights must exceed one H100 before KV cache")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    a100_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(a100_mem, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    weight_int4_gb_str = fmt_memory(weight_int4, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kv_headroom_gb_str = fmt_memory(kv_headroom, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kv_per_1k_sequence_gb_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_1k_sequence, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    max_1k_sequences_str = fmt_int(max_1k_sequences, commas=False)
    gpt3_int4_gb_str = fmt_memory(gpt3_int4, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
```

This comparison uses a conservative decimal HBM budget matching the A100 nameplate label, rather than the registered byte capacity used by the node estimator. A 70B model with 4-bit weights requires approximately `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.weight_int4_gb_str`, leaving `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.kv_headroom_gb_str` on an `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.a100_mem_gb_str` A100 for KV cache. With FP16 KV cache at about `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.kv_per_1k_sequence_gb_str` per 1K-token sequence for the MHA baseline, this supports about `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.max_1k_sequences_str` concurrent 1K-token sequences before other runtime overheads. With FP16 weights, the same 70B model would not fit on one A100 at all, so weight-only quantization changes both feasibility and batch capacity.

### Selecting a quantization format {#sec-inference-scale-quantization-selection-guidelines-24fb}

Choosing a quantization format from datasheet TFLOPS or nominal bit width alone fails when a 4-bit checkpoint degrades task accuracy on production prompts or when a smaller replica completes fewer SLO-compliant tokens per GPU. The final selection must satisfy memory, quality, and latency requirements together. Native support makes a precision path a candidate without establishing the model's quality at that precision, and no universal quality ordering separates 4-bit weight-only from 8-bit weight-and-activation quantization, so both are evaluated against the same task baseline. For compute-bound prefill, W8A8 offers the illustrated `{python} W8A8Ceilings.int8_ratio_mult_str` INT8 compute ceiling; for decode dominated by weight reads, W4A16 can cut the weight payload by up to 4$\times$, provided conversion and other costs leave a useful saving.

These precision choices affect cost per million useful tokens. The A100 residency calculation explains why fewer GPUs become possible at all, because INT4 weights shrink the resident payload enough for a 70B replica to fit on fewer devices. @Tbl-quantization-serving-cost isolates the effect of GPU count by assuming equal per-GPU prices and the same completed token rate across three configurations. Under that contract, reducing the number of billed GPUs reduces cost proportionally. The calculation does not establish that the smaller replicas sustain the same rate or meet the same quality and latency targets.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: quantization-serving-cost
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ QUANTIZATION IMPACT ON SERVING COST
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-quantization-serving-cost cost-per-1M-tokens table below.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that 4-bit quantization cuts serving cost in proportion to the
# │          GPU count it removes, not from per-GPU throughput gains.
# │ Show:    Cost per 1M tokens for FP16 (8 GPUs), AWQ 4-bit (4 GPUs), AWQ 4-bit
# │          (2 GPUs), scaled linearly from the FP16 baseline.
# │ How:     cost = baseline_cost × (gpu_count / baseline_gpus).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_usd

class QuantizationServingCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    baseline_cost = 2.40  # scenario assumption: FP16 cost per 1M tokens (estimated)
    baseline_gpus = 8  # FP16 on 8x A100
    gpus_awq_4 = 4  # AWQ 4-bit on 4x A100
    gpus_awq_2 = 2  # AWQ 4-bit on 2x A100
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    cost_fp16_8 = baseline_cost
    cost_awq_4 = baseline_cost * gpus_awq_4 / baseline_gpus
    cost_awq_2 = baseline_cost * gpus_awq_2 / baseline_gpus
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(cost_awq_4 - 1.20) < 1e-9, "AWQ 4-bit (4 GPU) cost should be \\$1.20")
    check(abs(cost_awq_2 - 0.60) < 1e-9, "AWQ 4-bit (2 GPU) cost should be \\$0.60")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    cost_fp16_8_str = fmt_usd(cost_fp16_8, precision=2, commas=False)
    cost_awq_4_str = fmt_usd(cost_awq_4, precision=2, commas=False)
    cost_awq_2_str = fmt_usd(cost_awq_2, precision=2, commas=False)
```

| **Configuration**               |         **Cost per 1M tokens (estimated)**         |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------:|
| **FP16 on 8$\times$ A100**      | `{python} QuantizationServingCost.cost_fp16_8_str` |
| **AWQ 4-bit on 4$\times$ A100** | `{python} QuantizationServingCost.cost_awq_4_str`  |
| **AWQ 4-bit on 2$\times$ A100** | `{python} QuantizationServingCost.cost_awq_2_str`  |

: **Quantization Impact on Serving Cost**: Estimated cost per million tokens at three configurations. At equal unit prices and unchanged useful token throughput, halving the GPU count halves the cost; halving it again brings the per-million-token cost to one quarter of the FP16 baseline. The cost savings come almost entirely from fewer GPUs rather than from per-GPU throughput gains. {#tbl-quantization-serving-cost tbl-colwidths="[58,42]"}

The illustrated 2--4$\times$ cost reduction follows from the assumed device-count reduction at unchanged useful throughput. If the smaller replica completes fewer qualifying tokens per second, cost per token falls by less and can increase. A deployment comparison must therefore combine billed replica cost with measured SLO-compliant output under the same quality contract.

Precision moves the capacity wall without removing it. A 175-billion-parameter model still needs about `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.gpt3_int4_gb_str` for its 4-bit weight payload alone, more than one `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` H100 holds before KV state and runtime allocations. Keeping that representation accelerator-resident requires distributing it across devices. Offloading to host memory is another placement choice, but introduces transfers that must fit the latency budget. Sharding addresses the capacity problem while adding communication and coordination to each replica.

## Model Sharding for Inference {#sec-inference-scale-model-sharding-inference-82b3}

When a deployment must retain a 70B model's `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_fp16_gb_str` of FP16 weights in accelerator memory, or when a 175B model's `{python} QuantizedServingCapacity.gpt3_int4_gb_str` INT4 weight payload still exceeds a single `{python} InferenceSetup.h100_mem_gb_str` GPU, no single accelerator can hold the replica. Where quantization shrinks the representation, sharding keeps it intact and divides it across multiple GPUs that execute together as one logical replica. The resulting design adapts tensor and pipeline parallelism from training, but must evaluate their communication and scheduling costs against per-request inference deadlines.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: hardware-setup-sharding
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HARDWARE SETUP: SHARDING (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-inference-scale-model-sharding-inference-82b3
# │
# │ Goal: Provide H100 memory capacity and the 70B FP16 weight footprint for
# │       the sharding-trigger calculation.
# │ Show: "80" GB; 70e9 x 16/8 = 140 GB; minimum 2-way sharding.
# │ How: Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity; Models.Language.Llama2_70B.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_display_math, fmt_int, fmt_memory_capacity, sci_latex

class HardwareSetupSharding:
    """Localized hardware reference for sharding."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_mem = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity
    model = Models.Language.Llama2_70B
    fp16_bits = int(BYTES_FP16.to(byte).magnitude * 8)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params = model.parameters.to(param).magnitude
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    min_shards = math.ceil((weights / h100_mem).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(min_shards == 2, "70B FP16 weights should need exactly 2-way sharding on 80 GB GPUs")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(h100_mem, unit=GiB, precision=0, commas=False)
    min_shards_str = fmt_int(min_shards, commas=False)
    weight_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{weights}}}} = {sci_latex(params, precision=0)} \times \frac{{{fp16_bits}}}{{8}} = "
        rf"{fmt(weights.to(GB).magnitude, precision=0, commas=False)} \text{{ GB}}"
    )
```

### Memory and latency triggers for model sharding {#sec-inference-scale-sharding-becomes-necessary-81d4}

A single-GPU replica fails when model weights overflow its HBM capacity or when its serial forward pass takes too long to meet the endpoint's TTFT and TPOT targets. Model sharding addresses the memory and latency rows of @tbl-distribution-triggers through different mechanisms, and the timing analysis below determines whether parallel execution repays its communication cost.

The first driver is memory capacity. If the selected representation must remain in accelerator memory but does not fit on one device, the replica needs multiple devices. For a model with $\Parameters$ parameters at precision $\NumericBitWidth$ bits, @eq-weight-memory gives the weight payload before metadata and runtime state:

$$\WeightMemory = \Parameters\times \frac{\NumericBitWidth}{8} \text{ bytes}$$ {#eq-weight-memory}

Applied to the 70B model in FP16 (16 bits), @eq-weight-memory recovers the payload quoted since @sec-inference-scale-singlemachine-serving-insufficient-3f13. Each parameter occupies two bytes, so the unquantized checkpoint alone requires:

`{python} HardwareSetupSharding.weight_display_math`

The result exceeds the `{python} HardwareSetupSharding.h100_mem_gb_str` capacity of an H100 GPU, establishing a weight-only lower bound of `{python} HardwareSetupSharding.min_shards_str` shards for an accelerator-resident replica. KV state, buffers, replication within the chosen partition, and uneven placement can require a larger degree.

The second driver is latency. Even when a model fits in memory, sharding can reduce latency by parallelizing computation. @Eq-parallel-time is the Fleet Law (@eq-fleet-law) applied to a single inference request, separating the compute term that sharding divides from the communication and synchronization terms it adds:

$$\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime$$ {#eq-parallel-time}

where $\DeviceCount$ is the number of devices in the sharding group, $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ is the communication overhead, $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ is synchronization overhead, and $\OverlappedTime$ is communication hidden behind useful compute. In the common no-overlap simplification with negligible extra synchronization, this reduces to $\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount+ \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$. Sharding provides latency benefit only when the nonoverlapped overhead is smaller than the time saved through parallelization.

### Tensor parallelism {#sec-inference-scale-tensor-parallelism-b29f}

Splitting every linear projection independently across GPUs would force an AllReduce synchronization after every matrix multiplication, stalling decode on interconnect latency. Tensor parallelism\index{Tensor parallelism!inference} [@shoeybi2019megatron] avoids half of those collectives by splitting each layer with the column-row partitioning\index{Tensor parallelism!column-row partitioning} developed for training. This keeps the activation between paired linear layers local and costs two AllReduce operations per transformer block, one after attention and one after the feed-forward sublayer.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Column-row tensor partitioning and its two AllReduce operations per transformer block are established in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-tensor-parallelism-d76e.
:::

The attention computation partitions across heads, so with $\AttentionHeadCount$ heads and tensor-parallel degree $\TensorParallelDegree$ each device computes attention for $\AttentionHeadCount/\TensorParallelDegree$ of them when the head count divides evenly. The KV cache is sharded\index{KV cache!tensor parallel sharding} with the heads, so each device stores cache only for its own heads. A multi-head attention layout spreads many KV heads across the group, while grouped-query attention with eight KV heads leaves one per device in an eight-way group.

```
8-way tensor parallelism, 64 KV heads (MHA):
Device 0: KV cache for heads 0-7
Device 1: KV cache for heads 8-15
...
Device 7: KV cache for heads 56-63
```

Cross-device reuse requires compatible cache content and placement. Matching tensor-parallel configurations can align the head partitions, but the receiver must also use the same model state, prefix inputs, cache representation, and logical token positions. A different partition requires redistribution rather than direct shard reuse. Equal parallelism degree alone does not establish cache validity.

Each device applies its shard of the attention output projection to its local heads, and an AllReduce\index{AllReduce!tensor parallelism synchronization} sums the projected partial outputs; its latency includes collective startup and coordination as well as payload transfer. @Fig-tensor-parallel-flow traces the resulting two synchronization points per layer across two GPU ranks.

::: {#fig-tensor-parallel-flow fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Tensor Parallelism for Inference**: Computation is distributed across devices by splitting tensor operations. Attention heads are partitioned across GPUs, requiring an AllReduce operation to synchronize results. Feed-forward networks use a column-row splitting strategy that requires only one AllReduce synchronization per block. This partition can reduce latency when saved compute exceeds communication cost, which is why the two collectives run over a fast local interconnect." fig-alt="Two columns labeled GPU 0 and GPU 1, separated by a dashed divider. In the attention stage, each GPU shows eight head tiles: GPU 0 holds the first four as solid tiles and draws the other four dashed, and GPU 1 holds the second four. From the bottom of each GPU's solid head tiles, labeled first or second half of heads, an amber arrow carries a partial output down into an AllReduce over NVLink bar. In the feed-forward stage, each GPU draws the matrix W1 split down the middle into columns, with its own column slice solid and the other dashed, labeled column slice of W1 plus activation. The matrix W2 is split across the middle into rows, with GPU 0 holding the top rows and GPU 1 the bottom rows, labeled row slice of W2 partial sum; on each GPU a blue arrow marked no communication runs from its column slice of W1 to the row slice of W2 it holds, GPU 1's arrow routing around the dashed top rows to enter its bottom rows from the side. Both partial sums feed a second AllReduce bar that leads to the next layer. A key reads held on this GPU for solid tiles and held on the other GPU for dashed tiles."}

![](images/svg/tensor-parallel-flow.svg){width="100%"}

:::

The inference time with tensor parallelism follows @eq-tensor-parallel-time:

$$\TensorParallelLayerTime= \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\TensorParallelDegree} + 2 \times \AllReduceCompletionTime(\CollectivePayloadSize)$$ {#eq-tensor-parallel-time}

@Eq-tensor-parallel-time is the per-layer instance of @eq-parallel-time. Here $\IronLawComputeTime$ is now the sequential compute time of one layer, and $\CollectivePayloadSize$ is the full activation payload each rank contributes to each AllReduce, priced by the ring cost model of @sec-communication-collective-operations-collective-operations-ring-allreduce-ffce. Compute divides ideally across ranks, but the reduced activation keeps its full shape, (tokens in the step) $\times$ (hidden width) $\times$ (bytes per element), and the factor of 2 counts the attention and feed-forward collectives (example \ref{exmp-inference-tensor-parallelism-llama-70b}). When a model spans multiple nodes without high-bandwidth NVLink across every rank, those two per-layer collectives become prohibitively expensive, motivating inter-layer pipeline partitioning instead.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Hiding tensor-parallel collectives behind compute on one node, and what that overlap can and cannot recover, is established in @sec-performance-engineering-overlap.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tp-speedup-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TENSOR PARALLELISM SPEEDUP CALCULATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Tensor Parallelism for Llama-70B" callout in
# │   §Tensor Parallelism for Inference.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute realized speedup (6.9×) vs theoretical (8×) for 8-way tensor
# │   parallelism on 8×H100, quantifying the communication overhead cost of
# │   AllReduce ops vs linear scaling.
# │ Show: tp_speedup_mult_str="6.9"x, seq_total_ms_str="2,400" ms,
# │   tp8_total_ms_str="348" ms, inline in the callout prose.
# │ How: Divide per-layer prefill-pass compute times; multiply by n_layers
# │   for full-model timing. This is not decode TPOT.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class TpSpeedupCalc:
    """Compute realized speedup vs theoretical for 8-way tensor parallelism on 8xH100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    _model = Models.Language.Llama2_70B
    # scenario assumption: per-layer phase timings (1 GPU vs 8-way TP)
    att_seq_ms = 12.0  # attention compute, sequential (1 GPU)
    att_tp_ms = 1.5  # attention compute, 8-way TP
    ff_seq_ms = 18.0  # feed-forward compute, sequential (1 GPU)
    ff_tp_ms = 2.25  # feed-forward compute, 8-way TP
    allreduce_tp_ms = 0.3  # AllReduce overhead per collective, 8-way TP
    tp_theoretical = 8  # linear scaling limit
    n_layers = _model.layers
    weight_fp16 = _model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    # Per-layer totals from the phase breakdown (two AllReduce ops per layer)
    seq_per_layer_ms = att_seq_ms + ff_seq_ms
    tp8_per_layer_ms = att_tp_ms + ff_tp_ms + 2 * allreduce_tp_ms
    tp_speedup = seq_per_layer_ms / tp8_per_layer_ms

    # Step 1: Full-model prefill-pass timing
    seq_total_ms = seq_per_layer_ms * n_layers
    tp8_total_ms = tp8_per_layer_ms * n_layers

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_params, fmt_time

    check(tp_speedup < tp_theoretical, f"Realized speedup ({tp_speedup:.2f}) must be less than theoretical ({tp_theoretical})")
    check(abs(seq_per_layer_ms - 30.0) < 1e-9, "per-layer sequential must sum to 30 ms")
    check(abs(tp8_per_layer_ms - 4.35) < 1e-9, "per-layer 8-way TP must sum to 4.35 ms")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tp_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(tp_speedup, precision=1, commas=False)
    seq_total_ms_str = fmt_time(round(seq_total_ms), 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=True)
    tp8_total_ms_str = fmt_time(round(tp8_total_ms), 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=True)
    parameters_b_str = fmt_params(_model.parameters, scale="B", precision=0, commas=False)
    weight_fp16_gb_str = fmt_memory(weight_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    seq_per_layer_ms_str = fmt_time(seq_per_layer_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    tp8_per_layer_ms_str = fmt_time(tp8_per_layer_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=2, commas=False)
    att_seq_ms_str = fmt_time(att_seq_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    ff_seq_ms_str = fmt_time(ff_seq_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    att_tp_ms_str = fmt_time(att_tp_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=1, commas=False)
    ff_tp_ms_str = fmt_time(ff_tp_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=2, commas=False)
    allreduce_tp_ms_str = fmt_time(allreduce_tp_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=1, commas=False)
```

::: {#exmp-inference-tensor-parallelism-llama-70b .callout-example title="Tensor parallelism for Llama-70B"}

**Scenario**: An engineering team deploys Llama-70B (`{python} TpSpeedupCalc.parameters_b_str` parameters, FP16 footprint `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.weight_fp16_gb_str`) across an 8-GPU H100 node with NVLink [@touvron2023llama2].

**Diagnosis**: The calculation assumes `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.seq_per_layer_ms_str` of serial layer compute as a reference, independent of the devices required to hold the weights: `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.att_seq_ms_str` for attention and `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.ff_seq_ms_str` for the feed-forward block. That reference describes a long-prompt prefill, in which every prompt token passes through the layer in one step, so it is far larger than one layer's share of a decode step on the reference replica. Ideal eight-way division gives `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.att_tp_ms_str` and `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.ff_tp_ms_str`, and the two AllReduce operations of @eq-tensor-parallel-time add an assumed `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.allreduce_tp_ms_str` each, for `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.tp8_per_layer_ms_str` per layer.

**Systems lesson**: The illustrative eight-way model gives a `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.tp_speedup_mult_str` reduction relative to its serial-compute reference (prefill time reduced from `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.seq_total_ms_str` to `{python} TpSpeedupCalc.tp8_total_ms_str`). The entire shortfall from the ideal 8$\times$ is the two collectives, a fixed cost per layer that dividing compute cannot shrink. Their share of the layer therefore grows as per-device compute falls, which is why a decode step, with far less compute per layer than this prefill reference, feels the collective cost most.

:::

### Pipeline parallelism for inference {#sec-inference-scale-pipeline-parallelism-inference-7ee3}

Splitting an 80-layer model sequentially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle during an isolated request and does nothing to shorten its forward pass. Pipeline parallelism distributes layers across devices so each stage runs a contiguous subset of layers and passes activations to the next stage without intra-layer synchronization.

For inference, pipeline parallelism creates bubbles\index{Pipeline parallelism!bubble overhead} differently than in training. Executing an isolated request serially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle at every step, whereas maintaining multiple in-flight requests fills the pipeline and amortizes the initial bubble across steady-state token delivery (@fig-pipeline-bubbles).

::: {#fig-pipeline-bubbles fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Pipeline Parallelism Bubbles**: (a) An 80-layer model split into four stages passes one request's activations from stage to stage, so splitting the layers alone does not shorten its sequential computation; it must still traverse all four stages. (b) With many requests in flight, later stages idle during the fill bubble, and from slot t4 onward every stage is busy and one request leaves the pipeline per slot. Pipeline parallelism therefore suits throughput-oriented serving better than latency-critical interactive serving." fig-alt="Two panels. Top: a request box, four stage boxes labeled GPU 0 to GPU 3 with layer ranges 1 to 20, 21 to 40, 41 to 60, and 61 to 80, and an output box, joined by activation arrows. Bottom: a grid of four GPU rows and seven time slots in which requests R1 to R7 enter GPU 0 one slot apart and shift one GPU down per slot. Hatched fill-bubble cells precede the first request on GPUs 1 to 3, and a dashed line at slot t4 marks the pipeline as full."}
